  • A Room Decoration Checklist: What Every Living Room Needs
  • Mirrors: The Underrated Room Decoration Tool

How to Make Your Living Room Feel Like Home

Creating a space that feels personal is one of the most rewarding parts of decorating. It’s about more than just filling a room with furniture. It’s about curating a collection of items that bring you joy and comfort.

Think of your living room as a canvas.

The sofa, coffee table, and shelves are the broad strokes, but the cosy living room accessories are the fine details that complete the picture. These small touches are where your personality comes to life.

Whether it’s a stack of your favourite books, a collection of photos, or a unique piece of art, these elements transform a generic room into a sanctuary that is uniquely yours.

This is one of the best approaches any home can adopt to feel more personal — and if you love rustic warmth, our guide to farmhouse living room styling ideas is well worth a read.

The Comfort of Cushions and Throws

I often think of textiles as the jumpers and scarves of interior design. They are, without a doubt, the easiest way to add instant warmth, colour, and personality to a room.

A bare sofa is just a piece of furniture, but add a few plush cushions and a soft throw, and it suddenly becomes an invitation to relax and get comfortable.


Shop Here

The key is to play with textures. For instance, you can create a rich, layered look by mixing a smooth velvet cushion with a chunky knit throw and a simple linen one.


Shop Here

This variety is not only visually interesting but also feels wonderful. A brilliant and budget-friendly tip is to do a 'seasonal refresh'.

In the summer, I swap my heavier wools for light cottons and linens to create an airy feel. Then, as autumn arrives, the cosy textures come back out. These simple swaps are fundamental accessories for living room decor that keep the space feeling fresh all year round. You can find some lovely options in our home textiles collection.

Textile Choices for Your Living Room
Material Feel & Style Best For Care Tip
Velvet Luxurious, soft, rich Adding a touch of glamour and depth Professional clean or spot clean gently
Linen Relaxed, airy, natural Creating a casual, breathable feel Machine washable, embraces a natural crinkle
Chunky Knit Wool Cosy, warm, textural Making a space feel snug and inviting Hand wash or dry clean to avoid shrinking
Cotton Versatile, soft, easy Everyday use and seasonal updates Generally machine washable and durable

Defining Your Space with Rugs

Rugs are the anchors of a living room. They have a wonderful ability to define a specific zone, like your main seating area, which is incredibly useful in the open-plan homes popular across the UK.

A well-placed rug pulls everything together, making the space feel cohesive and intentional. Here’s my most important tip for rug placement: ensure at least the front legs of your sofa and armchairs are on the rug.

SHOP HERE

This simple rule prevents the dreaded 'floating rug' look, where a small rug sits isolated in the middle of the floor, making the room feel disconnected. In fact, one of the most common mistakes I see is choosing a rug that’s too small. It can actually make a room feel smaller and more disjointed.

A generously sized rug makes the space feel more expansive and luxurious — for more inspiration on selecting the perfect option, take a look at our dedicated guide on elegant grey rugs and how to style them.

The pattern and colour can also be the thread that ties all the other accessories for living room decor together, from the curtains to the cushions.

Plus, you can’t beat the feeling of a soft texture underfoot for adding that final layer of comfort.

Expressing Yourself with Wall Decor

Now for my favourite part: wall decor. This is where you can truly let your personality shine, as art and wall hangings are the most personal of all accessories for living room decor. They are a direct reflection of your taste and story.


Shop Here

Creating a Focal Point

A single, large piece of statement art hung above a sofa or fireplace can instantly set the tone for the entire room. It acts as a powerful focal point, drawing the eye and anchoring the space.


Shop Here

Whether you choose a vibrant abstract piece, a calming landscape, or a striking black and white photograph, this one element can define your modern living room decor style.

Curating a Gallery Wall

If you have multiple pieces you love, a gallery wall is a fantastic way to display them. The key to how to accessorise a living room with a gallery wall is to create a sense of cohesion. I suggest choosing a theme, like family photos, travel memories, or botanical prints.


Shop Here

A crucial tip is to lay out your entire arrangement on the floor before hammering any nails. This allows you to play with the spacing and composition until it feels just right. You can even shop for art by colour to create a beautifully coordinated look. Don’t forget about mirrors, either. A large mirror can be a work of art in itself, with the added bonus of bouncing light around and creating an illusion of space—a brilliant trick for smaller living rooms.

Setting the Mood with Lighting

Lighting is so much more than just a utility; it’s one of the most impactful decorative features in a room. The secret to great lighting is to think in layers.

You need three types: ambient light (your main overhead fixture), task light (like a reading lamp by an armchair), and accent light (a small lamp to highlight a piece of art or a plant).


Shop Here

Floor and table lamps are like sculptures, acting as beautiful accessories for living room decor in their own right. The material of the base, whether it’s brass, ceramic, or wood, and the style of the shade contribute hugely to the room's aesthetic.

My game-changing tip? Install dimmer switches for your main lights. It’s a relatively small change that allows you to completely shift the room's atmosphere from bright and functional to soft and relaxing with a simple turn of a dial.

And never underestimate the simple magic of candles or fairy lights for creating a mindful, cosy evening glow.


Shop Here


Shop Here

Bringing Life Indoors with Greenery

I’m a huge advocate for plants as 'living accessories'. They are simply wonderful for adding life, natural colour, and a sense of calm to any space.

If you’re a beginner, I’d recommend starting with something hardy and forgiving like a Snake Plant or a Pothos. They thrive on a bit of neglect!

If you’re feeling more confident, a statement Fiddle Leaf Fig can create a stunning architectural feature. Crucially, remember that the planter is a decorative object itself.

Choose pots that complement your room's style, whether it’s a minimalist ceramic pot for a modern look or a rustic seagrass basket for a bohemian feel.


Shop Here

A few simple placement ideas can make a big difference. For example, try grouping smaller plants of varying heights on a windowsill or placing a trailing plant on a high shelf to create a beautiful cascading effect.


Shop Here

Showcasing Personality with Decorative Objects

These are the finishing touches, the little details that truly make a space unique and are perhaps the most personal accessories for living room decor. To avoid a cluttered look, I always follow the stylist's 'rule of three'.

When arranging items on a coffee table or shelf, group them in odd numbers (like three or five) and make sure to vary their height and texture.


Shop Here

A decorative tray is another secret weapon. It’s perfect for corralling small items like remote controls, coasters, and a candle, making them look tidy and intentional rather than messy.


Shop Here

Most importantly, don’t be afraid to display things that mean something to you.

  • Showcase collections: Whether it's vintage cameras or colourful ceramics, group them together for impact.
  • Display travel souvenirs: Let your decor tell the story of your adventures.
  • Frame personal items: A handwritten note or a child's drawing can become a piece of art.

This is how you weave your own story into your home’s design.

Stylish Shelving and Storage Solutions

I want you to start seeing storage not as a problem to be solved, but as a display opportunity.

Floating shelves, for example, can act as a mini-gallery for small art prints, plants, and your most treasured books.

I also love using stylish baskets made from wicker or seagrass. They are a chic way to hide away less sightly clutter, like children's toys or extra cables, while adding a lovely, natural texture to the room.


Shop Here

You can also have fun styling a 'shelfie'—artfully arranging your bookshelves by mixing books (some standing, some stacked) with decorative objects.

Ultimately, good storage is one of the most underrated accessories for living room decor, because an organised, clutter-free space is always a more calming and stylish one.

Putting Your Living Room Decoration Together

So, the real secret to a beautifully decorated living room is layering. It’s about combining different types of accessories—soft textiles, a defining rug, personal wall art, and warm lighting—to build a space that feels cohesive and deeply you.

There are no strict rules when it comes to how to accessorise a living room. The most important thing is to have fun with it and choose items that you genuinely love. After all, the best accessories for living room decor are those that reflect the stories and personalities of the people who live there, turning a simple room into a true sanctuary.

A Room Decoration Checklist: What Every Living Room Needs

One of the most helpful things you can do before buying any new piece is to work through a simple checklist. Position 3 competitors rank well precisely because they give readers a structured, actionable framework — and it works. Here's a practical room decoration checklist to guide your decisions:

Walls: Do you have at least one piece of art or a gallery arrangement that reflects your taste? A bare wall is a missed opportunity to add personality.

Rugs: Is your rug large enough that the front legs of your sofa sit on it? If not, consider sizing up to make the space feel cohesive.

Lighting: Do you have at least two light sources — one ambient, one accent — so you can adjust the mood in the evening?

Textiles: Have you layered at least two different textures across cushions, throws, or curtains to add visual warmth?

Greenery: Is there at least one plant or botanical element to bring freshness and life into the room?

Mirrors: If the room feels small or dark, have you considered a statement mirror to reflect light and add depth?

Candles or scent: Have you thought about how the room smells and the ambient warmth a candle brings when guests arrive?

Working through this list before you shop helps you spend intentionally, avoid impulse buys, and create a result that feels genuinely considered rather than cluttered. Browse our wall art collection to tick off the most impactful item on the list.

Mirrors: The Underrated Room Decoration Tool

If you've visited any well-ranked home decor resource recently, you'll have noticed mirrors appear consistently in their room decoration advice — and for good reason. A well-placed mirror does three things at once: it reflects natural light, makes the room feel larger, and acts as a decorative statement in its own right.

In a living room, the most impactful positions for a mirror are above a fireplace or console table, opposite a window to maximise light, or as part of a layered wall arrangement alongside artwork. A large, ornate frame can be as much of a focal point as a painting, while a simple round mirror suits more minimal schemes beautifully.

If your living room feels darker or smaller than you'd like, adding a mirror before buying any additional lighting is a smart, cost-effective first step. It's one of the most versatile and enduring home accessories available.

Competitor resources such as Anna Saxton's first apartment checklist address the total cost directly, which is why so many first-time renters land on those pages. A realistic starter budget for a furnished flat typically falls between £500 and £1,500 depending on the city and whether large furniture is needed.

The biggest savings come from prioritising ruthlessly: kitchenware, bedding, and cleaning supplies are non-negotiable from day one, whereas decorative items and specialist gadgets can wait. Charity shops, marketplace apps, and end-of-season sales can reduce your outlay significantly without compromising on quality where it matters.

A helpful way to plan is to divide your budget into three tiers — functional must-haves (roughly 60% of budget), comfort upgrades (25%), and personality touches such as wall art prints that make a rented space feel truly yours (15%). Keep a small medicine cabinet stocked with plasters, pain relief, antihistamines, and cold and flu remedies. A torch and a set of spare batteries are invaluable during power cuts. Have you ever walked into a room and felt it was missing something, a final touch to bring it all together? That missing piece is often the magic of home decor modern accessories. For me, these are the items that truly make a house feel like a home.

Quick Answer: Home decor modern accessories are the decorative accents — from sculptural vases and sleek trays to wall art and textured textiles — that give a finished, personal feel to any room. The Art of Placement: Creating Beautiful Focal Points

Once you've chosen your pieces, where you put them is just as important as what they are. I've learned a few simple design principles over the years that make a huge difference, and they're not as complicated as they sound. It’s all about creating little moments of beauty, or vignettes, that draw the eye.  

For an even more dramatic room refresh, pair your new accessories with our guide to DIY accent wall ideas to create a focal point behind your key furniture pieces.

  • The Rule of Threes: Have you ever noticed how items grouped in odd numbers just look better? It’s a classic trick. It creates a sense of balance that is more dynamic and interesting than an even-numbered group.
  • Layering for Depth: To create visual interest, think in layers. Place taller items at the back and shorter ones in front. You could lean a small piece of art against the wall behind a decorative box, for example. A beautiful set of framed wall pictures for living room can act as the perfect anchor for your vignette.
  • Using Negative Space: This is my favourite tip. Empty space is your friend! It gives your cherished items room to breathe. Resist the urge to fill every surface. This thoughtful approach allows each of your modern accessories to stand out and be truly appreciated, preventing a cluttered feel.

Wall Art as the Ultimate Modern Accessory

If I had to choose just one accessory to transform a room, it would always be wall art. I believe it's the most impactful of all home decor modern accessories.

Geometric prints and minimalist photography are also fantastic choices for a modern interior. Most importantly, choose something that speaks to you personally. Hanging art can feel daunting, but it doesn't have to be. Here are a few simple tips:

  • Hang at Eye Level: A common mistake is hanging art too high. The centre of the artwork should be at eye level, which is roughly 57 inches (or 145 cm) from the floor.

  • Consider the Scale: Make sure your art is the right size for your wall. A tiny print will get lost on a large wall, while an oversized piece can overwhelm a small space. As a general rule, art above a sofa should be about two-thirds the width of the sofa.

How to Shop for Modern Home Accessories: A Room-by-Room Guide

One of the most common questions people have when refreshing their home is simply where to start. Rather than buying accessories at random, a room-by-room approach helps you build a cohesive look without overspending or overcrowding your shelves.

Living room: This is your showpiece space. Focus on a statement sculpture, a curated tray for the coffee table, and a bold piece of wall art that anchors the room. A set of three varied-height vases in complementary tones is an easy win.

Bedroom: Here the priority is calm. Choose accents in muted tones — a ceramic bedside lamp, a woven throw, and a small framed print at eye level. Avoid cluttering surfaces; two or three thoughtfully chosen pieces work better than a shelf full of objects.

Home office: Functional accessories that also look good — a stylish desk organiser, a plant in a sculptural pot, and an inspiring print — help make the space feel personal

Modern vs. Traditional Accessories: Which Is Right for Your Home?

Choosing between a fully modern look and a more traditional feel — or finding a balance between the two — is one of the most common decisions when styling a home. Here is a quick comparison to help you decide.

Chinoiserie wall murals have captivated interior designers and homeowners alike for centuries, but with so many styles available today — from faithful reproductions to bold contemporary takes — knowing where to begin can feel overwhelming. Whether you're drawn to delicate botanicals, sweeping landscape panels, or intricate bird-and-blossom motifs, this guide will help you understand what chinoiserie is, why it endures, and how to style it with confidence in a modern British home.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

In the world of design, Chinoiserie Wall murals stands as a testament to the fascination with Asian motifs that has certainly persisted for centuries.

Quick Answer: Chinoiserie wall murals are decorative wall coverings or art panels that blend European and East Asian design traditions, typically featuring botanical motifs, pagodas, exotic birds, and landscape scenes. Originating in 17th-century Europe, the style remains popular today for adding elegance and visual depth to living rooms, bedrooms, and hallways. They work equally well as a single statement piece or across a full feature wall.

From Botanicals to yin-yang tables, this genre of reproduction design has indeed adorned everything from architecture to interiors, captivating Western audiences with its exotic allure. 

However, as we strive for inclusivity and cultural sensitivity in today's society, it's time to rethink Chinoiserie and consider how we can integrate this unique style into modern homes eaningfully.

Chinoiserie has a long and complex history, originating in 17th and 18th-century Europe as trade routes connected the continent to China for the first time. European aristocracy developed a taste for authentic Chinese goods, leading to a market of copycats and inspired designs. From Louis XIV's extravagant decor at Versailles to the adaptation of Chinese lacquer furniture by Thomas Chippendale, Chinoiserie certainly became synonymous with opulence and sophistication.

Today, Chinoiserie is experiencing a resurgence in popularity as part of the "grand-millennial" lifestyle aesthetic, blending shabby chic decor with nostalgic charm. Mass-produced items are readily available on many retailer stores. 

However, as we celebrate the beauty of Chinoiserie, it's essential to recognise the complexities and sensitivities surrounding its portrayal and interpretation. For many, Chinoiserie represents a Westernised fantasy of Asian culture, raising questions about authenticity, representation, and also cultural appropriation.

Rethinking Chinoiserie for Modern Homes

To integrate Chinoiserie into modern home decor thoughtfully, consider the following approaches:

1. Embracing authenticity

Pieces that honour and celebrate the craftsmanship and artistry of Asian cultures. Look for items inspired by traditional motifs and techniques rather than stereotypes. Choose pieces created in collaboration with Asian artisans or designers to ensure authenticity and integrity.

What Is Chinoiserie? A Brief History of the Style

Chinoiserie (pronounced shin-WAH-zer-ee) is a European decorative style that emerged in the 17th century, inspired by trade with China and a broader fascination with East Asian art and culture. The word comes from the French chinois, meaning Chinese, and describes a distinctly Western interpretation — rather than a faithful reproduction — of motifs such as pagodas, willow trees, exotic birds, and hand-painted botanical scenes.

At its height in the 18th century, chinoiserie adorned the palaces of Louis XIV at Versailles and influenced furniture makers including Thomas Chippendale, whose Chinese Chippendale designs remain collector's pieces today. The style is best understood as a creative dialogue between East and West: a European reimagining of Asian aesthetics that developed its own distinct visual language over centuries.

Today the style is enjoying a strong revival, particularly in UK interiors, where it brings an instant sense of heritage, depth, and craftsmanship to both traditional and contemporary spaces.

Chinoiserie Wall Murals vs Chinoiserie Wallpaper: What's the Difference?

Shoppers frequently search for both terms, and understanding the distinction helps you choose the right product for your space. Chinoiserie wallpaper is a repeat-pattern product designed to tile seamlessly across an entire wall or room, much like any traditional wallpaper. It is widely available, simple to hang, and easy to replace.

Chinoiserie wall murals, by contrast, are designed as a single continuous image — a panoramic scene that unfolds across one wall or a series of panels. Each mural is a standalone composition, which means the design does not repeat and the visual impact is far greater. Murals are particularly well suited to dining rooms, hallways, and bedroom feature walls where you want a truly immersive statement.

Art panels and prints offer a third option: framed or unframed chinoiserie-inspired artwork hung in a gallery-style arrangement. These give you flexibility to rearrange or add pieces over time and are a lower-commitment way to introduce the aesthetic into your home.

Which Rooms Suit Chinoiserie Wall Art Best?

Chinoiserie is remarkably versatile — its palette ranges from bold jewel tones to soft, neutral-toned panels that sit comfortably in almost any decorating scheme. That said, certain rooms benefit most from its particular qualities.

Dining rooms are the classic setting: a full-height mural wrapping the room creates an enveloping, theatrical effect that makes every meal feel like an occasion. This mirrors the historic use of chinoiserie in European aristocratic dining rooms.

Hallways and staircases are ideal for narrower panel arrangements. Because these are transitional spaces, a bold botanical or bird motif draws the eye naturally through the home without overwhelming it.

Living rooms work well with a single large statement panel or a curated set of chinoiserie-inspired art prints arranged as a gallery wall behind a sofa or above a fireplace.

Bedrooms suit softer, more muted chinoiserie palettes — pale grey or ivory grounds with delicate blossom and bird motifs create a calm, restful atmosphere without sacrificing character.

In conclusion, As we navigate the complexities of cultural representation in design, rethinking Chinoiserie offers an opportunity to celebrate the beauty and diversity of Asian art and heritage. By embracing authenticity, exploring contemporary interpretations, and supporting diverse voices, we can certainly integrate Chinoiserie into modern homes in a respectful, inclusive, and meaningful way. Knowing how to hang wall art correctly is one of the most overlooked skills in home decorating — yet it makes an enormous difference to how a room feels. Too high and the piece looks disconnected; too low and the whole wall feels unbalanced. Whether you're placing a single statement print or building a gallery wall from scratch, the decisions you make before you pick up a hammer will determine whether the result looks considered and intentional or slightly off.

To hang wall art like a pro, position the centre of each piece at 145cm (57 inches) from the floor, maintain 5–10cm gaps between pieces, and always use a spirit level and tape measure rather than guessing.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Key Takeaways

  • The centre of any wall art piece should sit at approximately 145cm (57 inches) from the floor to align with average eye level in most rooms.
  • Art hung above a sofa or sideboard should sit 10–15cm above the top of the furniture to feel connected rather than floating.
  • Gallery wall pieces should be spaced 5–10cm apart — consistent gaps create visual rhythm and prevent the display from looking cluttered.
  • Planning your layout on the floor or using paper templates before drilling prevents unnecessary holes and helps you find the best composition.
  • A spirit level and tape measure are non-negotiable tools — even a small tilt or miscalculation is immediately visible once the art is on the wall.
  • Art should span roughly two-thirds of the width of the furniture beneath it to maintain correct visual proportion.

Have you ever stood in front of a blank wall, artwork in hand, feeling completely unsure about where or how to hang it? You’re not alone. Over the years, I’ve worked with countless homeowners who face this exact challenge. With more than 12 years in home decor, I’ve seen how the perfect placement of wall art can transform a space — making it feel calm, inviting, and truly personal. On the other hand, I’ve often witnessed how hanging it just a little off-kilter or too high can throw the entire room out of balance.

There’s a real art to how we hang wall art. It involves more than just pushing a nail into the wall — it’s about creating a sense of harmony and style that complements your home’s character. I’m sharing practical guidance so you can hang wall art like a pro, avoid the all-too-common mistakes, and finally create that gallery-worthy look you’ve been dreaming about. Whether you’re refreshing your living room or working with decorative wall panels, you’ll find tips to plan, measure, and align your artwork with ease and confidence.

List of Contents

  • How High Should You Hang Wall Art for the Perfect View?
  • What Are the Best Ways to Measure and Align Artwork on Wall Panels?
  • What Spacing Rules and Layout Guidelines Should You Follow When Hanging Wall Art?
  • How to Create Balance When You Hang Wall Art
  • What Common Mistakes Should Homeowners Avoid When Hanging Wall Art?

How High Should You Hang Wall Art?

One question I often get from clients is, “How high should I hang my wall art?” Over time, I’ve found that the guideline of hanging artwork with the centre at roughly 145cm (57 inches) from the floor works beautifully for most rooms. This is close to average eye level and offers a comfortable viewing height whether you’re standing or sitting.

In living spaces where people tend to sit for long periods — like a lounge or dining room — you might want to hang art slightly lower, especially if the focal point is above a sofa or sideboard. I helped one client in Manchester rework their living room by lowering a large framed art piece by 10cm, which instantly made the room feel more inviting and well-balanced.

On the other hand, in corridors or stairwells where art is viewed standing up, sticking firmly to the eye-level centre works best. I often advise clients not to just ‘eyeball’ the height but to use a tape measure and make light pencil marks on the wall — and don’t forget to factor in the frame’s dimensions. The distance from the top of the frame to the hanging wire or hook also needs to be accounted for, as this is where many people make their first miscalculation.

Another tip I share is to consider the ceiling height. In rooms with high ceilings, you can afford to hang art a little higher, but don't exceed 165cm from the floor to the centre of the art. It's also worth thinking about choosing the right frame size for your artwork before you start measuring — an oversized or undersized frame changes how the piece reads on the wall. This keeps your wall art within a natural line of sight and maintains the room’s flow.

Once everything is level and secure, the final step is making sure your display stays looking its best — read our full guide on caring for your wall art once it's in place, from safe cleaning methods to the best spots for long-term preservation.

Quick Height Checklist for Hanging Wall Art

  • Standard eye level centre: 145cm from floor
  • Above seating: 10–15cm above furniture
  • In corridors and staircases: maintain eye level
  • In rooms with high ceilings: max 165cm centre height

What Are the Best Ways to Measure and Align Artwork on Wall Panels?

Working with wall panels can elevate a room’s character but also requires a bit more precision when you hang wall art. Many homeowners don’t realise that the panels’ grooves and sections should guide your artwork placement rather than interfere with it.

One common mistake I see on site is clients hanging art that cuts awkwardly across wall panel joints or installs pieces off-centre within the panel space. This spoils the overall aesthetic and creates visual clutter. When I consult with clients on using wall panels, my first step is always to map out the panels on paper, noting their dimensions and spacing.

To hang wall art successfully here, measure both the panel and the artwork’s frame. Align the artwork within the panel’s centre zone, or allow the panel lines to frame the art naturally. A spirit level is essential — never guess. It’s also worth marking the centre of the panel with a light pencil cross before you do anything else, as this gives you a fixed reference point for all subsequent measurements.

Here’s a simple table to help you organise your measuring and alignment process:

Step Action Tools Needed Pro Tip
1 Measure width and height of wall panel Tape measure Note panel moulding and joint placement
2 Measure artwork frame dimensions Tape measure Include frame thickness
3 Mark centre of panel on wall Pencil, spirit level Use a laser level for precision
4 Mark hanging points based on frame’s hanging system Measuring tape, pencil Double-check height from floor
5 Install fixings ensuring level art Drill, screws, spirit level Use appropriate fixings for wall type

Keeping this methodical approach ensures your artwork fits naturally within the panel layout, enhancing both the panels and the art itself.

What Spacing Rules and Layout Guidelines Should You Follow When Hanging Wall Art?

Spacing wall art correctly can be the difference between an organised, calming space and a cluttered mess. Over the years, many clients have tried hanging multiple pieces unevenly, resulting in a chaotic display that detracts from their interior style.

  • Keep 5–10cm between individual pieces to create breathing space but keep the display unified.
  • Maintain at least 15cm clearance between art and nearby furniture so your art doesn’t feel crowded.
  • When arranging a gallery-style wall, plan the layout on the floor first — this helps visualise proportions and spacing before you commit.

Many clients I’ve worked with have benefited from using paper templates or painter’s tape on the wall to outline art dimensions. This trick avoids unnecessary holes and helps discover the best composition visually. It also gives you the freedom to step back and assess the arrangement from across the room before a single nail goes in.

Also, consider scale carefully. Small artworks need grouping to avoid looking lost, while oversized pieces should often be a standalone focal point. A single large piece can anchor an entire wall and create a calm, considered atmosphere that a cluster of small prints rarely achieves on its own.

Example: Living Room Wall Art Layout

A recent project for a couple in Leeds involved hanging three framed prints above their sofa. Initially, they planned to space the pieces 3cm apart, which felt too tight. After rearranging to maintain 7cm gaps, the wall art suddenly looked balanced and inviting. The small adjustment made an enormous difference to how the whole room felt — proof that spacing is one of the most underestimated decisions in any hanging project.

How to Create Balance When You Hang Wall Art

Good styling principles provide a foundation for integrating wall art within your room’s overall design language. As someone who’s worked with scores of clients, I’ve noticed that understanding these principles leads to interiors that feel purposeful and calming.

For example, the “rule of thirds” or “golden ratio” can help position wall art in a way that feels naturally pleasing to the eye. This means dividing your wall or room visually and aligning major art pieces at the intersections to create balance. It sounds technical, but in practice it simply means avoiding the instinct to centre everything symmetrically — a slightly off-centre arrangement often feels more dynamic and alive.

Many homeowners I advise get great results by considering their room’s existing colour palette and texture when choosing art. A piece with too many clashing colours can overwhelm a peaceful space. Instead, I guide clients to pick artworks that complement fabric textures or the tones of furniture, so the art feels like it belongs rather than competes.

For a calming effect, layering artworks with reflective qualities such as glass frames or muted tones works beautifully. Mixing frame materials — such as wood and metal — creates subtle contrasts that add interest without disrupting the room’s overall sense of calm. Browse our range of unique wall art to find pieces that complement your existing palette and furniture.

What Common Mistakes Should Homeowners Avoid When Hanging Wall Art?

One of the most frequent errors I spot is hanging wall art too high. A client in Bristol once proudly showed me a large statement art piece they hung nearly 30cm above eye level. Though well framed, the placement made the space cold and disconnected from other room elements.

Another mistake is ignoring furniture height. Art should relate to the proportions of sofas, beds, or consoles beneath it. I always say, art above furniture should have a gap of about 10–15cm — too tight and it feels cramped, too far and the art seems disconnected.

Some homeowners also try to cram too many different art styles or frames on one wall without a unifying theme or colour palette. This often results in sensory overload rather than harmony. A simple fix is to commit to one frame colour or material across all pieces, which instantly brings order to even a large and varied collection.

I recall advising clients in Edinburgh who had a wall filled with mismatched prints and photos. We resolved it by keeping just a few favourites in frames of the same colour, then repositioning them with equal spacing using a gallery grid layout. The change was transformative — the room suddenly felt organised and relaxing.

Lastly, inadequate tools can cause misalignment. Don’t underestimate a good spirit level and appropriate wall fixings. Over time, I’ve seen artworks droop or fall because nails were placed in the wrong spots or too shallow. For heavier pieces, always use wall anchors or locate a stud — the few extra minutes this takes will save you from a very costly mistake.

By avoiding these pitfalls and using the techniques shared here, your walls will become an expression of style and serenity. For further inspiration, browse our framed wall pictures for the living room and find pieces that suit your space perfectly. You can also find unique home decor to complete the look around your newly hung art.


Shop Here

To DIY or Hire a Professional? Knowing When to Call for Help

Most wall art can be hung confidently at home with the right tools and a little patience — a tape measure, spirit level, and appropriate fixings are all you really need for the majority of prints, canvases, and framed pieces. Where things get more complicated is with very heavy items, oversized canvases, or walls that are tiled, made of solid concrete, or covered in plasterboard without obvious studs.

If your artwork weighs more than 10kg, or if you are drilling into an unfamiliar surface, it is always worth consulting a professional handyperson. The cost is modest compared to the risk of a piece falling and causing damage — either to the wall or to the artwork itself. Similarly, if you are arranging a large gallery wall across an entire room, a second pair of eyes (and hands) makes the process significantly easier and more accurate.

For most everyday pieces, however, the guidance in this article is all you need to achieve a result that looks polished and intentional. Start with lighter pieces to build your confidence, use painter's tape templates to plan before you drill, and work methodically rather than rushing the process.

Choosing the Right Hanging Method for Your Wall Type

The fixing method you choose matters as much as where you place your artwork. Different wall surfaces require different approaches, and using the wrong one is one of the most common reasons pieces shift, tilt, or — in the worst cases — fall.

Plasterboard walls: Use hollow-wall anchors or specialist picture hooks rated for your artwork's weight. Avoid standard nails, which have very little grip in plasterboard and will pull through over time.

Solid brick or masonry walls: A masonry drill bit and wall plug followed by a screw will give you the most secure fixing. This takes a few more minutes to set up but is by far the most reliable method for heavier pieces.

Tiled walls: Use a tile drill bit and proceed slowly to avoid cracking the tile. If the artwork is light enough, damage-free adhesive strips designed for tiles are a practical no-drill alternative.

Adhesive strips and hooks: Brands such as Command offer damage-free hanging solutions that work well for lighter pieces on smooth, painted walls. Always check the weight rating and follow the manufacturer's instructions exactly — surface preparation is critical for adhesive products to hold reliably.

When in doubt, check the weight of your artwork and match it to a fixing rated above that weight. A little extra care at this stage prevents damage to both your walls and your artwork.

To Wrap Up

Hanging wall art might seem straightforward, but the difference between a thoughtfully placed piece and a randomly hung one is enormous. Using proper measuring, alignment, and spacing methods — especially when working with features like wall panels or specific room proportions — is key to creating beautiful, balanced interiors. Every home is unique, so take time to reflect your personal aesthetic whilst following these guidelines. Happy decorating!

Minimalist art is one of those concepts that feels instantly recognisable — a single bold shape, a whisper of colour, a canvas that seems almost empty yet commands a room. But what is minimalist art, exactly, and why does it have such a profound effect on the spaces we live in? At its core, it is a movement that emerged in 1960s America, championing the idea that art should strip away the non-essential and let pure form, line, and space do all the talking. Far from being cold or sparse, the best minimalist pieces carry an extraordinary sense of intention and calm.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

This art form — pared back, quietly powerful, and rooted in simplicity — so often creates an instant sense of calm when you walk into a room. I’m willing to bet that peaceful feeling didn’t come from a space cluttered with fussy décor. More often, it comes from a deliberate choice to embrace simplicity—and this is where the power of minimalist art truly comes to life.

For me, minimalist art isn’t about cold or empty spaces. Instead, it’s about using clean lines, simple shapes, and a quiet colour palette to make a surprisingly strong statement. It’s art that doesn’t shout for attention; it confidently holds its own, creating a sense of order and tranquillity. In this article, I want to share my love for this art form and show you how it can influence our homes.

Together, we’ll explore how choosing the right piece can help you curate a space that feels both effortlessly stylish and wonderfully serene. It’s all about creating a feeling—not just decorating a wall.

The Core Principles of Minimalist Art

To truly appreciate this style, it helps to understand the simple ideas that make it so impactful. It’s less about what’s there and more about how the few elements present work together. Think of it as a visual deep breath for your walls.

Simplicity and Form

At its heart, minimalist art is about stripping away everything non-essential. It celebrates the pure beauty of a shape or line. Imagine comparing a highly ornate, carved chair with a perfectly crafted, simple wooden one. The simple chair’s beauty comes from its clean form and function, and the same is true for this art style. It invites you to appreciate the elegance of a single curve or the strength of a straight line, free from any visual distractions.

Colour and Repetition

You’ll often notice that minimalist pieces use a monochromatic or very limited colour palette. This isn't a lack of imagination; it's a deliberate choice. By using just one or two colours, the artist allows the form and texture to become the main focus. Furthermore, the repetition of simple shapes or lines can be incredibly soothing to the eye, creating a sense of rhythm and harmony that feels both orderly and peaceful.


Shop Here

The Beauty of Negative Space

Perhaps one of the most important elements is what isn't there. Negative space, the empty area around the subject, is crucial in this style of work. It gives the artwork room to breathe and prevents your eyes from feeling overwhelmed. This space encourages your mind to rest and focus, making the entire composition feel balanced and intentional. It’s a quiet pause in a visually busy world.

The Artists Who Shaped the Minimalist Movement

So, who do we have to thank for this beautifully simple style? While the movement has deep roots, a few key artists truly defined its character, and their influence is still seen everywhere in modern interior design UK.

Donald Judd, for instance, created what he called "specific objects," which were often beautifully simple boxes made from industrial materials. You can see his influence in the clean lines of modern metal-framed shelves and furniture. His work taught us that form itself could be the art.

Then there’s Agnes Martin, whose work I think of as whispers on a canvas. Her subtle grids and pale colour washes create an incredibly meditative feeling. Her art is perfect for anyone seeking a piece that encourages quiet reflection, much like the feeling we want in a peaceful bedroom.

Similarly, artists like Frank Stella and Dan Flavin explored bold geometry and the power of light. Stella’s shaped canvases and graphic prints are direct ancestors of the bold abstract art for home we love today. Flavin went a step further, using standard fluorescent light tubes to create entire installations. He proved that even an everyday object could become a stunning piece of minimalist art when presented with intention.

Bringing Tranquillity into Your Home with Minimalist Wall Art

For me, a home should be a sanctuary, a place to unwind and recharge. This is where minimalist art truly shines. By choosing art that is simple and uncluttered, you are essentially helping to declutter your walls and, in turn, your mind. Think about the difference between a busy gallery wall with dozens of images and a wall anchored by one large, serene abstract print. The single piece commands attention without creating visual noise, establishing a clear focal point that anchors the room. This approach creates a sense of order and provides a restful backdrop for your daily life — and if you are still working out which aesthetic suits you best, our guide to finding your home decor style is a great place to start.

This aesthetic ties directly into the growing desire for wellness and mindfulness in our living spaces. Creating calming home decor is about more than just picking pretty things; it’s about making conscious choices that support your mental wellbeing. A piece of minimalist art can be a powerful tool in this process. It encourages you to pause and appreciate subtlety, transforming a simple wall into a source of calm. If you're looking to create a focal point in your main living space, exploring a curated selection of framed pictures for the living room can be a wonderful place to start finding that perfect, peaceful piece.

How Minimalist Art Affects Your Mood and Wellbeing

How does a piece of art actually make you feel? It’s a question worth asking when choosing something for your home. By removing complex scenes and distracting details, minimalist art encourages a different kind of engagement. Your mind isn't working hard to interpret a story or identify objects; it can simply be with the artwork. This quality allows for a sense of focus and reflection. The clean lines and uncluttered compositions can have a genuinely calming effect on our nervous system, which is often overstimulated.

This makes minimalist art ideal for specific functions within the home. For example, a piece with bold geometric shapes can enhance concentration in a home office, while a soft, monochromatic canvas can promote restfulness in a bedroom. Some people find the style a bit cold, but I see it as a matter of personal connection. The key is to choose a piece that speaks to you. For some, that's a quiet whisper of colour; for others, it's a bold, clean statement. The right piece of minimalist art will always feel just right.

Practical Ways to Style Your Space with Minimalist Wall Art

Now for the fun part: bringing it all home! Knowing how to style minimalist art is easier than you think. It’s all about letting the artwork have its moment. Here are a few simple wall art ideas to get you started, room by room.

The goal is to match the artwork to the function and feeling of the space. A large, dynamic piece of minimalist art can bring energy to a social area, while a smaller, more subtle work can create a pocket of calm in a quiet corner. Don't be afraid to leave plenty of white space around the art; it's part of the look! To help visualise this, I’ve put together a little table with some starting points.

The History and Origins of Minimalism in Art

Minimalism did not arrive quietly. It emerged in the United States in the late 1950s and early 1960s as a direct and deliberate reaction against the emotional intensity of Abstract Expressionism — the movement of Jackson Pollock's frenetic drip paintings and the brooding colour fields of Mark Rothko. Where Abstract Expressionism was charged with feeling and personal gesture, minimalism insisted on objectivity, industrial precision, and the complete removal of the artist's hand.

The movement was also a response to the visual noise of consumerism and Pop Art. Artists wanted to create work that existed purely on its own terms — not as a symbol, not as a narrative, and not as a vehicle for emotion. A Donald Judd stack of aluminium boxes was simply what it was: material, form, and space. This radical honesty gave minimalism its authority and continues to make it feel fresh decades later.

By the mid-1960s, minimalism had a name, a critical framework, and a generation of artists committed to pushing its boundaries. Judd's 1965 essay Specific Objects is widely regarded as the movement's founding text, arguing that the most interesting new work existed somewhere between painting and sculpture — occupying real space rather than representing it. This thinking underpins every clean-lined abstract wall art print you see in contemporary homes today.

Minimalism in Art vs Minimalist Interior Design

It is easy to use these two terms interchangeably, but there is a meaningful difference worth understanding — particularly when you are trying to build a cohesive home aesthetic. Minimalism as an art movement is a specific historical category: works created from the 1960s onwards by artists such as Judd, Martin, Flavin, and Stella, governed by the movement's strict rejection of representation and personal expression.

Minimalist interior design, by contrast, is a broader and more flexible aesthetic philosophy. It borrows the movement's visual language — clean lines, neutral palettes, deliberate negative space — and applies it to the way a room is arranged and furnished. A minimalist interior does not need to hang historically certified minimalist art; it simply needs pieces that share the same visual calm: simple geometric forms, monochromatic tones, and an absence of decorative clutter.

In practice: you do not need to own a Judd or a Martin to achieve a minimalist home. A set of carefully chosen minimalist wall art prints that echo the movement's principles — restrained colour, clean geometry, generous space — will have exactly the same effect on a room's atmosphere.

What exactly are earthy neutrals, and why do so many interior designers turn to them when creating a genuinely restful home? Put simply, they are the warm, grounded tones borrowed from the natural world — terracotta, mushroom brown, muted ochre, and soft moss — that work together to make a space feel settled and human. Unlike cooler, trend-driven palettes, these hues have a timeless quality that works across a huge range of UK home styles, from a compact city flat to a sprawling country cottage.

Have you ever walked into your home after a long day and wished it felt more like a peaceful retreat? I certainly have. Often, the secret to creating that sense of calm lies in the colours that surround us.

This is where the magic of earthy neutrals comes in. This palette is so much more than just beige. Instead, think of the rich, complex colours you’d find on a walk in the woods: deep terracotta, gentle moss green, soft mushroom browns, and muted ochre. These are the foundational shades for creating organic home colour palettes.

Learning how to use warm natural tones is about borrowing directly from the outdoors to bring a sense of grounding and peace inside. These hues have a wonderful psychological effect, helping to reduce stress and reconnect us with the natural world.

A calm home environment can also beautifully support other wellness practices, like the tapping meditations from Feed Your Spirit, which help foster inner peace. The versatility of these organic hues is fantastic, as they work with so many styles, from modern minimalist to the rustic charm of Japandi decor.

The real beauty, however, appears when you begin to combine them with texture and art.

Creating Depth with Layered Tones and Textures

A common worry with a neutral palette is that it might look flat or uninspired. I promise you, that couldn’t be further from the truth!

The key is to create depth by layering different shades and, most importantly, textures. Imagine painting your walls in a light, airy taupe.

Now, place a sofa in a deeper mushroom shade in front of it and add cushions in a rich, warm rust.

This approach is central to creating authentic nature inspired home decor. Each material brings its own character and feeling to the space.

Balancing Warmth with Light and Greenery

One question I get asked a lot is how to stop a room with warm tones from feeling too dark or heavy. It’s a valid concern, but one that’s easily solved with a few simple tricks. First, let’s talk about light.

You want to maximise every bit of natural light you have. I suggest using sheer linen curtains that allow sunlight to filter through softly. Placing a large mirror opposite a window is another classic trick that works wonders to bounce light around the room.

Next, think about your artificial lighting in layers.

You need ambient light from a ceiling fixture, task light like a reading lamp by a chair, and accent light to highlight something beautiful, like a piece of art.

This combination creates a warm and balanced glow in the evening.

Finally, bring the outside in!

Greenery is absolutely essential for these calming colour schemes for living rooms. A tall fiddle-leaf fig in a corner or a few small succulents on a shelf add a vibrant pop of life and colour.

These are simple yet effective biophilic design ideas that reinforce that connection to nature. As a final touch, add a few reflective surfaces, like glass vases or some of our beautiful framed pictures with brass frames, to catch the light and add a subtle touch of elegance.

Using a grounded colour scheme doesn’t mean you have to play it safe. In fact, you can make a powerful statement.

One of my favourite ways to do this is by creating a feature wall. Painting the wall behind your bed or sofa in a deep, moody moss green or a rich rust can instantly anchor the room and create a stunning focal point.

Another bold move is to choose a large piece of furniture as your colour statement. An ochre velvet sofa, for example, can become the warm, inviting heart of your living room. 

From there, you can shop for art by colour scheme to find pieces that harmonise perfectly. But making a statement doesn't always have to be loud.

Sometimes, the most impactful statements are the quietest. You can create a deeply sophisticated and serene look by layering many similar earthy neutrals.

Think of a room dressed in various shades of mushroom, taupe, and sand. The harmony of these closely related tones creates a cohesive and calming atmosphere that feels incredibly chic.

If you’re a little hesitant to commit to a bold wall or sofa, I suggest starting with textiles. A large rug or a set of curtains in a strong natural hue can completely transform the feel of a room, giving you a chance to experiment without a big commitment.

With a backdrop of warm, natural tones, you have so many beautiful options. For a calming, organic feel, I love pairing these walls with abstract art that features soft lines and a complementary palette.
